In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the 33‐GHz source counts are complete in the flux density range 20–114 mJy.
the VSA has demonstrated that it is a useful instrument for the study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies at high frequency and for the study of the properties of radio sources at 33 GHz.
the VSA source subtraction strategy is effective in removing the vast majority of sources in the VSA fields, and that the 33-GHz counts are consistent with those from previous studies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the VSA is the first instrument that can measure the CMB power spectrum at a frequency above 20 GHz.
the VSA has made a significant contribution towards understanding the radio background.
the VSA has provided the first detection of a cosmic microwave background anisotropy at 33 GHz, and has measured the source counts at this frequency.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the source counts are not as steep as previously thought.
the VSA source subtraction strategy was successful in reducing the contribution from bright radio sources to the VSA data.
it is possible to use a single baseline to subtract sources from interferometer observations, even for a relatively large field of view.
